My family has farmed this land in Quzhou for generations. I know this soil and this climate — the flat plains, the dry winters, the summer rains. I have about 10 mu of contracted land. There is only one thing I would plant: winter wheat and summer maize, the same rotation my father did and his father before him. I am 64. My knees bother me. I am not going to experiment with cotton or vegetables — those need too much hand labor and the prices jump around too much. Wheat and maize I know. The grain station buys them reliably.

For wheat, I sow in October after ploughing. I use the improved Jimai variety that the county extension office has been promoting for years — it yields well here and I trust it. I apply compound fertilizer at planting, then spread urea at jointing in March. I will irrigate four times: before sowing to prepare the seedbed, once at wintering, once at jointing, once at heading. The water table is deep here but I have well access. I spray herbicide once in winter and a fungicide before heading — powdery mildew has been bad the last few years.

For maize, I direct-seed into the wheat stubble right after the June harvest — no time to plough, and the county man told me no-tillage holds the moisture. I use Xianyu 335 hybrid seed, the same one everyone around here uses. Summer rains usually handle irrigation, but I will pump once in August if it turns dry. One herbicide pass early, one spray for corn borer if I see it bad.

I keep the inputs roughly the same as last year. I do not reduce fertilizer because I cannot afford a bad yield.
